overview:
Two revolutions happened in Russia in the same year, and the confusion is compounded by the calendar: Russia still used the Julian reckoning, thirteen days behind the West, so the February Revolution fell in March and the October Revolution in November by the dates most of the world was keeping. The first began in Petrograd in late February 1917 as bread queues, a women's demonstration and factory strikes that the garrison was ordered to suppress and instead joined. Within a week the three-hundred-year Romanov dynasty was finished; Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March (15 March), and his brother declined the throne. What replaced him was not one government but two overlapping ones — a Provisional Government drawn largely from the liberal Duma, and the Petrograd Soviet of workers' and soldiers' deputies, whose Order No. 1 gave it effective command of the capital's troops. Contemporaries called the arrangement dvoevlastie, dual power, and it never resolved.

The Provisional Government's fatal choice was to stay in the war. Russia had already lost enormous numbers of men to German and Austrian offensives, the railways and grain supply were failing, and peasants had begun seizing land without waiting for permission. Lenin, returned from Swiss exile in April through German-arranged transit, argued against any support for the government and for power to the soviets — a position that looked marginal in spring and much less so by autumn. A botched summer offensive, the July Days rising that briefly drove Lenin into hiding in Finland, and then General Kornilov's murky march on Petrograd in August, which Kerensky survived only by arming the Bolshevik-influenced workers' militias, steadily drained the government of authority and handed it to its rivals. On the night of 25 October (7 November), Red Guards and sympathetic sailors took the bridges, telegraph and stations, and arrested the ministers in the Winter Palace with far less fighting than the later official mythology depicted.

Holding power proved far harder than taking it. Elections to a Constituent Assembly, held in November, gave the Bolsheviks roughly a quarter of the vote behind the peasant-based Socialist Revolutionaries; the assembly met once in January 1918 and was dispersed by armed guards the next day. The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 bought peace with Germany at the cost of Poland, the Baltics, Finland and Ukraine, and the surrender split the revolutionary coalition. What followed was a civil war of Reds against Whites, nationalist movements and foreign expeditionary forces from Britain, France, Japan and the United States, fought across an enormous territory and accompanied by requisitioning, terror on both sides, epidemic and famine that together killed millions. By 1922, when the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was proclaimed, the Bolsheviks had won — over a country in ruins.
significance: The events of 1917 created the first state to define itself by Marxist revolution, and for the next seventy-four years that state was a pole of world politics — a model, a patron and a threat. It pulled Russia out of the First World War and freed German divisions for the Western Front; it produced an alternative to liberal capitalism that shaped anti-colonial movements from China to Vietnam to Cuba; and it frightened Western governments enough that fear of Bolshevism coloured their tolerance of the European right in the 1920s and 1930s. It also established, in the dispersal of the Constituent Assembly, the one-party state and the machinery of the Cheka, a template of revolutionary dictatorship that would be copied widely and would leave the question of whether October was a popular rising or a coup contested for a century.
coverage: The dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is drawn from it; the account comes from reference works and institutional pages retrieved in this session, and the map can show none of it in place or time. The wider record is unusually contested rather than thin: Soviet historiography rewrote 1917 to inflate Lenin's and later Stalin's roles and to present October as inevitable, émigré and Cold War accounts read it as a conspiracy by a small disciplined party, and the post-1991 archive openings supported a messier picture of a fractious Bolshevik party riding events it did not fully control. Casualty figures for the civil war and famine years, the actual scale of German funding to the Bolsheviks, and the depth of popular support for the October seizure all remain estimates or arguments rather than settled facts.
